title: In-situ observation of variant pair formation in bainite of low carbon steel by digital holographic microscopy
abstract: Digital holographic microscopy (DHM) was employed to investigate the formation process and shape evolution of the most frequently observed bainite variant pairs in low-carbon alloy steel. Through in-situ observation coupled with theoretical predictions, the continuous changes in surface relief corresponding to bainite and adjacent austenite were measured. Additionally, the crystal orientations of the observed variant pairs were determined using electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD). The results indicated that at the onset of the transformation, the bainite variant shape agreed with theoretical predictions, while the adjacent austenite experienced plastic deformation. However, as the transformation proceeded towards completion, the shape of some bainite variants deviated from the theoretical predictions, while their adjacent austenite remained undeformed. This shift of deformation strain between austenite and bainite suggests a change in strain accommodation mechanism. Furthermore, the observed ‘tent-shaped’ surface relief was attributed to back-to-back mutually accommodating variant pairs, resulting in reduction of the total shape strain, compared to the theoretical prediction.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Bainite structures have been gaining increasing attention for their good balance of strength, toughness, and creep resistance in the latest advanced high-strength low-carbon steels. Such mechanical properties are highly dependent on their microstructure consisting of lath-shaped ferrite with high dislocation density and fine cementite particles. Since the thickness of bainite and the substructure of bainite, including packet and block, are both considered to strongly affect the mechanical properties [ 1 ], there has been extensive research on the substructure of bainitic steels.

A packet is an aggregate consisting of ferrite laths with habit planes (HP) nearly parallel to each other, while a block is that consisting of ferrite lathes with close crystallographic orientation. Bainite has been reported to hold a specific crystal orientation relationship with its prior austenite, which is near Kurdjumov-Sachs (K-S) orientation relationship (

The correspondence between bainitic and its prior austenite is almost identical to those associated with martensite reactions. Therefore, there has been a long debate about whether bainite transformation is consistent with martensite transformation [ 2–5 ]. Nevertheless, the crystallography of upper bainite and lath martensite are quite like each other and will be discussed together below.

There have been reported several different kinds of packet and block structures in bainite and martensite [ 6–8 ]. On some occasions, variants sharing the same parallel closed-packed planes form together, while in other situations, variants having the same Bain correspondence with prior austenite (

                      ) form together. In the case of the closed-packed group, packets consisting of two variants with the smallest misorientation tend to form at higher temperatures, while all six variants in the same closed-packed group tend to form at lower transformation temperatures. In addition, an increased number of twin-related variant pairs is usually observed with decreased transformation temperature [ 9 ]. In the case of the Bain group, it is reported that a specific pair of variants of the Bain group without sharing the same closed-packed plane tends to form. The almost equivalent variant paring tendency has been reported even in martensite [ 10 ]: Variants within the same Bain group are preferentially formed in IF steel, while variants within the same closed-packed plane are preferentially formed in 0.75 wt.% C steel. Therefore, transformation temperature, as well as carbon concentration, are both believed to influence variant selection tendency.

Such a variant selection tendency has been discussed from the viewpoint of different accommodation processes of transformation strain, i.e., plastic accommodation by the deformation of austenite matrix, or self-accommodation by interaction and cancellation of strain from multiple variants. Kundu [ 11 ] demonstrated that based on the interaction of residual stress in austenite and shape deformation of martensite, variant selection of thermally induced martensitic transformation from cold-deformed austenite could be predicted. Similarly, Jafarian et al. [ 12 ] proved that different variant selection exists for coarse/ultra-fine grain austenite, which can additionally be explained by the restriction by prior austenite grain boundaries. However, the experimental evidence of the accommodation process is limited. Most research on variant growth is based on statistical data obtained only after the completion of the phase transformation. Therefore, a direct observation of certain variant pair formation will provide new insights into understanding the variant selection mechanisms.

Strain and shape deformation of martensite and bainite variants will lead to surface relief of the material. Hence, surface relief is of great importance in understanding the variant selection. Traditionally, surface relief associated with these transformations has been observed by either atomic force microscopy (AFM) [ 13 ], scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) [ 14 ], or Confocal Laser Scanning Microscopy (CLSM) [ 15 ]. While AFM and STM offer exceptional sub-nanometer resolution to sub-nm scale, their scanning systems limit them to post-transformation observation. On the other hand, CLSM allows for continuous observation of surface relief evolution during transformation. However, CLSM lacks the capability for quantitative analysis in the continuous observation mode. Moreover, although invariant plane strain (IPS) surface relief is confirmed in bainite, tent-shaped surface relief which contradicts the IPS is also observed [ 16 , 17 ]. Therefore, a more in-depth understanding of surface relief is necessary.

Being the first to apply digital holographic microscopy in this field, our research group has demonstrated its potential as a powerful tool for making quantitative, real-time observations on the evolution of surface relief during bainite and martensite transformation [ 18 ]. This approach provides a unique opportunity to visualize the transformation and deformation behavior of metals in real-time and in three dimensions, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of their mechanism. In the present study, surface relief induced by the single variant of martensite/ bainite, and bainite variant pairs in low-carbon alloy steel was measured. Based on the observation, the effect of plastic accommodation and self-accommodation of transformation strain is evaluated, and the mechanism of variant selection is discussed in detail.

sections.heading: Experimental methods
paragraphs:
Low-carbon alloy steel which has superior hardenability is chosen for this research. Its composition is shown in  Table 1 
                      . Martensite transformation start (M s ) temperature and bainite transformation start (B s ) temperature are calculated based on the equations proposed by K. Ishid [ 19 ] and Y. K. Lee [ 20 ], respectively.

Specimens with the size of 2 mm×2 mm×2 mm were cut from rod specimen and then mirror polished and set in an infrared heating box filled with Ar/H 2  atmosphere. The heat treatment includes drying at 100 ℃ for 10 min and austenitization at 1200 ℃ for 4 mins, followed by Ar/H2 gas quench at a cooling rate of approximately 20℃/s. This specific quenching process has the potential to induce the formation of both martensite and bainite structures, so the structures to be observed were selected deliberately. The temperature profile throughout the process was measured by a thermocouple directly attached to the specimen. For clarity and consistency in the DHM figures, the growth initiation time of the target phase was designated as 0 s.

During the whole cooling process, surface relief change was measured using DHM with a laser wavelength of 640 nm and frame rate of 20 fps. The detail of the DHM system can been found elsewhere [ 18 , 21 ]. Afterward, the same area observed by DHM was analyzed using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) by a JSM-7200F scanning electron microscope with a step size of 0.3 µm. During the continuous cooling, both martensite and bainite could be transformed. Martensite and bainite are distinguished by differences in formation speed, so the observation and analysis are selectively focused on martensite or bainite. In this study, plates observed to form within a single frame (less than 0.1 s) were categorized as martensite, while plates captured to grow over multiple frames (usually more than 1 s) were classified as bainite. This is also adopted in previous research for the in-situ observation of bainite surface relief [ 22 ].

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: The formation of variant pairs is widely recognized as a mechanism to accommodate the invariant plane strain associated with displacive transformation, leading to a shift in the observed frequencies of different variant pairs [ 29 ]. The gradual growth characteristic of bainite allows for the observation of the variant pair formation process, potentially providing valuable insights into the underlying selection tendencies governing variant selection. This study will investigate the formation process, surface relief changes, and strain accommodation behavior of the most frequently observed bainite variant pairs, V1/V8, V1/V4, and V1/V2, listed in descending order of their transformation temperatures. However, to gain deeper insights into the mechanisms governing these phenomena, we will begin by analyzing single variants of both martensite and bainite.

sections.heading: Growth of martensite single variant
paragraphs:
The Pole figure corresponding to the martensite grew within the target prior austenite grain is shown in  Fig. 3 
                         . The habit plane and shape deformation direction of V1 are indicated in  Fig. 3 (b). The trace of the habit plane is shown as the red curve. DHM observations on the growth of martensite V1 are shown in  Fig. 4 
                         (a)–(c). From  Fig. 4 (a) to (b), martensite surface relief, designated as M1, emerged within 0.2 s at a temperature of approximately 370 ℃. Subsequently, from  Fig. 4 (b) to (c), another martensite surface relief, named M2, emerged on the right side of M1. For a better understanding of the martensite and adjacent austenite, a 3D representation of surface relief corresponding to martensite M1 is provided in  Fig. 4 (d).  Fig. 4 (e) illustrates the line profile along a cross-section of M1 and M2, as Indicated in  Fig. 4 (a)–(c). At 0.41 s, a noticeable upheaval in surface relief, covered by a yellow overlay, distinctly exhibits the features of IPS, indicating its clear martensitic feature. On the contrary, on the left-hand side of the martensite, a gradual but uneven slope, which represents deformed austenite, was observed. Similar methods of assessing surface relief were also reported in previous studies [ 13 , 30 , 31 ]. The measured slope of both M1 and M2 and the slope predicted for V1 by PTMC are compared in  Fig. 4 (f). Both M1 and M2 were in good agreement with the prediction, which means the formation of martensite is not restricted. The primary accommodation mechanism for the martensite single variant involves plastic deformation of austenite on one side of the martensite. This also aligns with prior research that measured lattice distortion of retained austenite using EBSD [ 32 ].

sections.heading: Growth of bainite single variant
paragraphs:
Fig. 7 
                          shows the surface relief change induced by the growth of bainites. In  Fig. 7 (a), a bainite sheaf named B was halfway grown at a temperature near 450 ℃. Sheaf B later reached the prior austenite grain boundary indicated by the white dot line in  Fig. 7 (b). Subsequently, another sheaf, B’, emerged as shown in  Fig. 7 (c). The EBSD analysis confirms that both B and B’ belong to the same variant, V1. Unlike martensite, bainite grows at an observable speed that typically takes several seconds to reach a fixed shape. Previous research [ 22 ] suggests that bainite growth is anisotropic, and the anisotropy potentially impacts surface relief. For instance, if bainite grows upwards from below the surface, the initial transformation stages could involve a mixture of thin bainite tips and surrounding austenite. This initial morphology might exhibit a lower slope compared to the PTMC prediction. However, with continued expansion, the slope may gradually approach the prediction. In this specific case, the growth direction is inclined around 45° from the surface. Accordingly, a relatively slower slope growth is expected.  Fig. 7 (d) shows the 3D shape of bainite sheaf B.  Fig. 7 (e) illustrates the evolution of the surface relief profile along the cross-section indicated by white lines in  Fig. 7 (c). At 1.12 s, a gradual upheaval appeared within the area highlighted in yellow. Subsequently, at 1.57 s, the upheaval steepened and solidified in shape, indicating the formation of the bainite sheaf B. On the other hand, on both sides of sheaf B, surface relief characterized by subsidence and uplift are observable in the red highlighted area. At 2.92 s, the left-hand side of B thickened in width, while on its right side, sheaf B’ emerged in the deformed austenite. The slope of B and B’ are shown in  Fig. 7 (f). Similar to martensite, the bainite single variants are in good agreement with PTMC prediction and the strain accommodation for bainite single variants is also a plastic one. However, unlike martensite, austenite deformation is evenly distributed on both sides of the bainite sheaves.

sections.heading: Formation of bainite variant pair V1/V8
paragraphs:
Fig. 8 
                         (a) indicates the IPF map of upper bainite formed at approximately 460 ℃. The selected prior austenite, outlined by the white dotted line, is depicted in the reconstructed prior austenite grains as shown in  Fig. 8 (b). In  Fig. 8 (c), the highlighted sheaves indicated by yellow and red correspond to V1 and V8, respectively. In the target prior austenite grain, a V1 sheaf named as B1 was first formed from a prior austenite grain boundary, and a V8 sheaf named as B2 subsequently emerged adjacent to the first formed V1 sheaf, forming a V shape. After that sheaf B1 thickened and finally reached the apparent width of around 6–8 μm. As indicated by the blue dot line in  Fig. 8 (c), sheaf B1 might consist of multiple grains (subunits) with a similar orientation. Since variants V1 and V8 belong to different closed-packed plane groups, their habit planes are different as shown in  Fig. 9 
                         .

To gain a deeper understanding of the morphology of the V1/V8 pair, a 3D illustration of the V1/V8 pair is provided in  Fig. 9 (e) and (f). Notably, the habit planes of V1 and V8 are not parallel to each other. Consequently, the close-packed direction shared by the two variants is their only junction part, geometrically. If the observation surface is not parallel with the close-packed direction, the junction part of the V1/V8 pair will be restrained to the tip of the ‘V shape’ on the surface, as shown in  Fig. 9 (f). This also explains why previous research often observed a scattered V1/V8 boundary.

Fig. 10 
                         (a) and (b) present the raw DHM images illustrating the surface relief induced by two bainite sheaves of variants V1 and V8, captured from the same field analyzed by EBSD. The V1 sheaf elongated over time similarly to a single variant. Subsequently, the V8 sheaf nucleated in the vicinity of the tip of the V1 sheaf from the plastically deformed austenite and elongated in a different direction from the V1 sheaf, forming a V shape between the two variants. For a clearer understanding of the surface relief shape and corresponding variants,  Fig. 10 (c) presents the 3D representation of the V1 and V8 sheaves within the area enclosed by the white line in  Fig. 10 (b). The bainite indicated by arrows appears smooth and even, representing a typical shape of a displacive transformation product. Furthermore,  Fig. 10 (d) and (e) display the quantitative measurement of the cross-sectional profile in  Fig. 10 (c). The slope of the V1 sheaf plateaued within only 0.92 s. The V8 sheaf exhibited the same behavior, and the final slopes measured for both variants agree well with the PTMC predictions. The relatively faster slope growth as compared to that of the single variant might be attributed to the difference in the growth direction. In this case, both of the growth directions of V1 and V8 are almost parallel to the surface, as indicated by their closed-packed directions in  Fig. 9 .

sections.heading: Formation of bainite variant pair V1/V4
paragraphs:
Fig. 11 
                         (a) and (b) display the IPF map of upper bainite and reconstructed prior austenite, respectively. The black dotted line indicates part of the prior austenite grain. In  Fig. 11 (c), sheaves B1 and B2, highlighted in yellow, are designated as variant V1 for further analysis. These sheaves nucleated from the prior austenite grain boundary, located upper right in the figure, at a temperature of approximately 440 ℃. Then, they elongated downwards in the figure until encountering another bainite sheaf already formed along the prior austenite grain boundary at the bottom of the figure. The V1 sheaves thickened over time. Subsequently, within the deformed austenite located between the V1 sheaves, sheaves corresponding to variant V4, highlighted in green, formed. Notably, V1 and V4 formed adjacent to each other in most of the observed areas.

Fig. 13 
                         (a) and (b) display the raw DHM images of the surface relief induced by the formation of sheaves B1 and B2. B1 appeared earlier on the surface than B2, which grew in parallel at a distance approximately two or three times the width of B1. The 3D representation of the surface relief induced by the formation of these bainite sheaves is shown in  Fig. 13 (c). Similar to the V1/V8 pair, the smooth area corresponds to the bainite sheaves, while the uneven area represents the surrounding deformed austenite. For a quantitative understanding of the surface relief profile and corresponding variants, height measurements along the cross-section are provided in  Fig. 10 (d), (e), and (f).

The growth of sheaf B1 began with an upheaval observed at 0.87 s. This upheaval continued to steepen from 0.94 s to 1.36 s. Plastic deformation was observed on both sides of sheaf B1 during their growth, while thickening occurred specifically to the right. The steepening of sheaf B1 eventually plateaued as depicted in  Fig. 13 (d). Afterward, although the thickening of the sheaves continued on one side from 1.36 s to 2.65 s, its slope remained nearly constant. In contrast, the initiation of V4 growth was less apparent initially. However, the slope of the plastically deformed area in the vicinity of V1 gradually restarted to increase, as indicated in  Fig. 13 (e) and (f). This increase reached a maximum by 7.58 s, and remained stable at 8.3 s. Besides, the interface between V1 and V4 was stationary throughout the growth of V1 and V4. The bainite sheaves exhibited a continuous thickening behavior throughout the entire transformation process.

The evolution of the slopes for variants V1 and V4 is shown in  Fig. 14 
                         , where the yellow and green dots represent the slopes of variants V1 and V4, respectively. The solid lines indicate the corresponding predicted values by PTMC. V1 exhibited a rapid initial increase in slope over the first 2 s, before reaching a constant value that closely aligns with the prediction. This observation aligns with our previous research [ 18 ], where the slope induced by a single-variant bainite sheaf was observed to reach the predicted value gradually. Conversely, the slope of variant V4 increased much slower than V1, and only reached a stable value after a significantly longer time, coinciding with the completion of the entire transformation. Interestingly, this slope of V4 was slightly higher than the predicted value by approximately 0.02. This discrepancy suggests that variant V4 was formed from deformed austenite. However, the exact timing of the actual transformation initiation for V4 remains unclear.

sections.heading: Formation of bainite variant pair V1/V2
paragraphs:
Fig. 16 
                         (a) and (b) show the evolution of the surface relief of bainite sheaves B3 and B4, their transformation temperature was around 420 ℃. The two sheaves are formed parallel to each other, while thickening continued even after their lengths reached maximum. A 3D representation of the surface relief for sheaves B3 and B4 is presented in  Fig. 16 (c), along with quantitative measurements of the cross-sections in  Fig. 16 (d) and (e). B3 initially exhibited nearly equivalent slopes on both sides, which gradually increased over time. This symmetrical surface relief resembles the ‘tent-shaped’ bainite reported in the previous research [ 16 , 17 ]. On the other hand, as depicted in  Fig. 16 (e), plastic deformation of surrounding austenite is less pronounced, unlike all the other cases. Additionally,  Fig. 16 (f) shows that the final slopes of both V1 and V2 are much lower than the prediction by PTMC, which is also different from all the other cases.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: In this research, the growth behavior of single martensite/bainite variants and frequently observed variant pairs in bainite have been investigated. A single bainite variant exhibits a strong crystallographic resemblance to martensite: the influence of IPS on surface relief is confirmed, and the final shape after transformation is in good agreement with the prediction by PTMC.

The same principle also applies to the V1/V8 pair: V1 forms similarly to a single variant. Subsequently, V8 nucleates adjacent to the tip of V1, forming a small junction plane. V8 also grows in a manner similar to a single variant. Accordingly, the shape strains induced by both V1 and V8 are plastically accommodated within the parent austenite grain.

The formation behavior of variant pairs of V1/V4 is illustrated in  Fig. 17 
                      (a). In the case of the V1/V4 pair, V1 first grows similarly to a single variant, inducing plastic deformation in the surrounding austenite. As V1 continues to grow, its slope approaches the PTMC prediction with obvious thickening in one direction. In contrast, in the area where V4 will eventually form, the subsidence slowly thickens. The slope of this region does not reach the PTMC prediction until the end of the transformation. This suggests that V4 takes much longer to reach its final shape compared to V1, or that formation of V4 takes place only at the final stage of the transformation. Several factors might influence this delayed formation of V4: (1) Shape deformation of V1 activates specific slip systems in the surrounding austenite, making it more favorable for V4 to nucleate later. (2) The presence of V1 might limit space or restrict the deformation state of the remaining austenite, hindering the formation of other variants and allowing only V4 to develop. (3) Hardening the surrounding austenite makes it more difficult for V4 to nucleate and grow. Despite the delayed formation, V4 ultimately contributes to accommodate overall shape deformation strain. The overall austenite deformation around V1/V4 was found lower than that around V1/V8.

The formation behavior of variant pairs of V1/V2 is illustrated in  Fig. 17 (b). In the case of the variant pair V1/V2, both variants start growing simultaneously and their expansions are uniform. Furthermore, both V1 and V2 exhibit similar slopes, resulting in symmetrical surface relief. However, the measured slopes are only one-third of the PTMC prediction as shown in  Fig. 16 (f), clearly indicating the reduction of the overall strain component. Moreover, subsidence/upheaval in adjacent prior austenite grain is not prominent, which indicates that plastic deformation in austenite is limited. Both factors, as well as the conversed shape deformation direction of V1 and V2 as shown in  Fig. 15 (e), suggest that the transformation strain is accommodated within these variants.

The reason for different variant formation tendency in this study can be explained from several aspects such as (1) autocatalytic nucleation [ 31 ], and (2) self-accommodation which satisfy the kinematic compatibility (KC) condition [ 32 , 33 ]. While both theories contribute to understanding variant selection under specific conditions, distinguishing their applicability is crucial for variant pairs V1/V8, V1/V4, and V1/V2.

sections.heading: Autocatalytic nucleation
paragraphs: Bainite nucleation can be categorized into grain boundary nucleation and autocatalytic nucleation [ 33 ]. Ashwath M. Ravi [ 33 ] proposed that grain boundary nucleation dominates during the initial stage of bainite transformation, but autocatalytic nucleation will be more efficient during the later stage. Such theory is highly consistent with the in-situ observation: for the occasion of V1/V8, V1 was initially nucleated on the prior austenite grain boundary, and later V8 nucleated on the V1 grain boundary sharing a very small junction plane parallel to the shared close-packed direction. Both variants grow in a manner like single variants. In the case of V1/V4, V1 nucleation also occurred on the prior austenite grain boundary, and it elongated continuously like a single variant as well. However, V4 nucleation took place adjacent to the V1 grain boundary, but it was discontinuous along the length direction.

Given the fact that further bainite nucleation is accelerated by γ dislocations originating from the strain by V1, Furuhara et al. proposed that V4 and V8 are mostly favored [ 7 ]: V1 and V4 share the same slip plane, while V1 and V8 share the same slip direction, thus the shape strain shared to γ will also facilitate lattice invariant shear during further transformation. Based on EBSD analysis, both V4 and V8 nucleate on the boundary of V1, supporting the above assumption. However, the stress induced in the surrounding austenite is different between V4 and V8: the formation of V8 is likely to increase the stress further, while V4 can partially relax the stress induced by V1. The earlier formation of V8 indicates that the V/V8 variant pair is the most favored under weak mechanical constraints. However, under strong constraints, such as those depicted in  Fig. 13  where the same variants developed close together, V4 becomes the only viable option due to the limited space available.

sections.heading: KC condition
paragraphs:
Compatibility has been considered a crucial factor determining the variant clustering behavior, for incompatibility usually leads to elastic stress, plastic deformations, or the existence of a transition layer [ 34 ]. When two variants with different shape strains are continuously connected at the junction plane, a rigid body rotation is needed. The magnitude of rigid body rotation is the degree of incompatibility [ 35 ]. Therefore, the smaller the degree of incompatibility is, the lower the energy required for the formation of a variant pair. Calculations of incompatibility of all the variant pairs in carbon steel, based on double-shear PTMC [ 35 , 36 ] have shown that for lath martensite, variant pair V1/V2 has negligible incompatibility. In the same way, the KC condition between V1 and other variants of bainite has been calculated based on the method given by K. Bhattacharya [ 37 ]. The junction plane and incompatibility indicated by Q are shown in  Table 4 
                         . Variant pair V1/V2 satisfy the KC condition better than any other variant pairs, which is in good agreement with previous research. The actual junction plane between V1 and V2 is confirmed in  Fig. 18 
                         . In  Fig. 18 (a) white dot line represents the trace of the junction plane, which indicates a sharp coherent interface. The traces of the junction plane in the IPF map ( Fig. 18 (a)) and the PF ( Fig. 18 (b)) show good agreement.

In contrast to the other variant pairs, the surrounding prior austenite grain adjacent to the V1/V2 variant pair exhibited no apparent plastic deformation. This suggests that strain accommodation for the V1/V2 pair is restricted within the two variants themselves. One possible explanation is that two variants influence each other through the mutual cancellation of shape deformation. Since V1 and V2 have nearly equal thicknesses, the combined shape deformations remain parallel to the shared close-packed direction. As both variants are confirmed to grow simultaneously, this residual deformation needs to be counterbalanced. The activation of slip systems within V1 and V2 might be a potential mechanism for this counterbalance, leading to the observed decrease in slope for both variants.

The misorientation angle between variants V1 and V2 exhibits a remarkably close agreement with theoretical predictions based on the K-S relationship, with a difference of less than 0.3°. In contrast, other variant pairs, such as V1/V4, show much larger deviations ranging from 4° to 5° from the K-S prediction. These observations suggest the closely aligned orientation of shape deformation directions and slip directions in the neighboring variants might have influenced each other. As shown in  Fig. 18 , the shape deformation direction of V1 nearly aligns with the slip direction of V2, and vice versa. These slip systems might have been activated to counterbalance the shape deformation, and potentially result in the observed decrease in slope of both variants.
Therefore, the cancellation between shape deformation of both V1 and V2 could be achieved through in-plane slip, and the lattice including the habit plane and junction plane is not rotated.
However, the reason why the slip systems parallel to the close-packed direction are not activated remains unclear and remains to be clarified in further research.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
For the first time, the growth sequence, nucleation behavior, and surface relief change of the most frequently reported bainite variant pair are captured by in-situ DHM observation. Combining PTMC prediction, the reason for variant pair selection was discussed as well. The conclusions are as follows. 
                         
                            1. 
                            Different growth sequences exist for variant pair V1/V8, V1/V4, and V1/V2 in bainitic transformation: for the V1/V8 and V1/V4 variant pairs, after the formation of a plate of V1, a formation of V8 or V4 followed in both cases. V8 nucleates adjacent to the tip of V1 and elongates instantly, while V4 nucleates on the side of V1 and thickens. In the case of the V1/V2 pair, their nucleation occurred on the grain boundary and grew simultaneously. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            The slope of the surface relief induced by the signle martensite/bainite variant is in good agreement with the PTMC prediction. Slopes induced by variants pairs V1/V4 and V1/V8 are also consistent with the prediction expected for the V4, which shows an influence of plastic deformation of prior austenite. On the contrary, variant pair V1/V2 exhibits a slope much lower than the PTMC prediction. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            Strain accommodation of V1/V8 is similar to a single variant that fully relies on plastic accommodation in the prior austenite. Nevertheless, V1/V4 first relies on plastic deformation of γ matrix, but later growth of V4 also helps further accommodation. The shape strain of the ‘tent-shaped’ V1/V2 was reduced by self-accommodation, and the surface relief was reduced due to the deformation of both variants.

sections.heading: Difference in variant selection tendency between surface and bulk
paragraphs:
To quantify the potential difference in variant selection between the surface and bulk regions, the variant selection frequencies at the surface and in the bulk of the low-carbon steel were investigated based on the EBSD analysis. The sample underwent the same preparation method and temperature profile employed throughout the present study. The EBSD analysis was first conducted on the surface. Subsequently, after removing a surface layer with a thickness of 200 μm, the EBSD analysis was applied to the underlying bulk material.
